newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Oilseeds - Korea to buy, Taiwan demand slows.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Oilseeds - Korea to buy, Taiwan demand slows.

text.p: South Korea's feed milling companies are expected to buy several thousand tonnes of feed meal ahead of a report by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) on planting intentions next week, traders said on Monday.
But soybean imports by Taiwanese buyers are seen sliding due to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease which has devastated its multi-billion dollar pork industry, the dealers said.
"There are some (KOrean) buyer groups who want to cover their requirements ahead of (the) USDA report next Monday," a trader with one of the feed mills in Korea said.
The National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) in Seoul has invited tenders for 50,000 tonnes of cottonseed meal by 0200 GMT on Wednesday for July to November delivery.

Dealers said the Korea Feed Association was also expected to seek about 50,000 tonnes of soymeal this week, and the Big Feed Mills are likely to buy 20,000-30,000 tonnes of tapioca for shipment from May onward.
Korean edible oil producers are also looking at picking up 50,000 tonnes of U.S. No.2 soybean for prompt April shipment.
In Taiwan, the ban on pork exports would probably lead to a 10 percent fall in soybean imports as demand for processed soymeal to be used as animal feed drops, dealers said.
"We don't see much demand for soymeal now, so we must reduce our soybean imports," Taiwan Formosa Oilseed manager Steven Kuo told Reuters by telephone.
"We may not have pigs to eat our soymeal, but soyoil demand remains," Kuo said. "A 10 percent cut in imports is likely."
Japan, where Taiwan controls up to 45 percent of the pork market, and South Korea have already imposed an indefinite ban on the importation of pork products from Taiwan.
Oilseed buyers in Japan and the Philippines, however, will be sidelined this week, traders in both countries said.
Japanese buyers are already well covered on soybeans, including material coming from South America and do not need to go into the market at the moment, traders said.
"We're checking Chicago market and cash prices in the U.S., but had no big business recently," a soybean trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
The Philippines, which buys about 20,000 tonnes of soybeans a month, will also be sidelined this week due what buyers there feel are high prices in the United States, dealers said.
